assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a new platform in which a single twist angle tunes flat-band electronic structure, producing correlated insulators, superconductivity and later Chern and fractional states. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted flat bands from first principles-style reasoning and the experiments then confirmed the prediction, a clean theory-experiment arc that fits how I judge electronic-structure ideas. The field it spawned (moire matter) is large and conceptually original.
assessment.attribution: The theoretical prediction rests clearly on Bistritzer and MacDonald, and the first experimental demonstration of correlated and superconducting behaviour on Jarillo-Herrero's group. The credited trio gives a natural split, though the experimental first author Yuan Cao is not among the supplied names and I cannot resolve how the committee would treat that.
assessment.maturity: Independent replication by many groups across several years is strong, and the basic band-flattening picture is stable. Recognition is timely; some higher-order phenomena (the origin of superconductivity) remain debated but do not undermine the core discovery.
uncertainties: Origin of the superconducting pairing remains unsettled.
Credit for early twisted-graphene theory (other groups) and the experimental first author is not captured by the credited names.
I am relying on memory for dates and priority and have not verified them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the workhorse for treating strongly correlated electrons, bridging band theory and local many-body physics, and underlies LDA+DMFT calculations of Mott transitions, heavy fermions and correlated oxides. It is original, mathematically clear and has lasting impact on how real materials are computed. This is directly in my field, so I weigh it carefully rather than favourably by default.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar established the mapping to an impurity problem and the practical framework. Among the supplied names Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt form a defensible trio, but Metzner and others (Muller-Hartmann, Jarrell) are not credited and the allocation of priority is a real issue.
assessment.maturity: More than three decades of use, extensions (cluster DMFT, DFT+DMFT) and agreement with spectroscopy support maturity. Quantitative accuracy for specific materials remains method-dependent, but the framework is firmly established.
uncertainties: Priority among the founders (Metzner, Muller-Hartmann, Jarrell) is contentious.
The prize would reward a method, and its quantitative predictive power varies by system.
Facts about priority come from my memory, not independent verification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, and later giant TMR with crystalline MgO barriers, enabled modern read heads and MRAM. It is a physically transparent spin-dependent tunnelling effect with very large technological impact, following the logic of the giant magnetoresistance prize.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin (and Yuasa and Djayaprawira's group) delivered the MgO giant TMR and its industrial realisation. Giving credit to Parkin for MgO is plausible but shared with Yuasa and others who are not credited; the trio is reasonable but not unambiguous.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are heavily replicated and in large-scale commercial use for years, so maturity is high. Recognition is arguably overdue given the 2007 GMR precedent and the device record.
uncertainties: Credit for MgO-barrier giant TMR is distributed among several groups.
The Julliere 1975 precedent and theory (Butler, Mathon) complicate the narrative.
Dates and priority are from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction and observation of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators created a field of symmetry-protected topological electronic matter, with edge and surface states protected by time-reversal symmetry. Originality and conceptual impact are very high, and many computational materials searches rest on it.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the foundational theory; Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe and Molenkamp's group observed it; Hasan and others identified 3D topological insulators. The three-person cap forces hard choices and the BHZ contribution is not supplied among the names, which makes a fair allocation difficult.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent experiments confirm the effect, though quantisation is less perfect than in the integer quantum Hall regime. The field overlaps heavily with the 2016 prize (topological phase transitions) and recognition is timely but allocation is contested.
uncertainties: Several decisive contributors (BHZ, Fu, Kane, Moore, Balents; Hasan) cannot all be included.
Overlap with the 2016 topological-matter prize.
Potential experimental imperfection of edge conduction.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2008 discovery of superconductivity in iron pnictides at 26 K and its rapid rise above 50 K opened a second high-temperature superconductor family with multiband, magnetically proximate physics, challenging the cuprate-only picture. It is a clear experimental discovery whose significance is easy to state.
assessment.attribution: Kamihara and Hosono reported LaFeAsO(1-x)Fx; the credit is cleanly assigned to two people. Follow-up discoveries of higher Tc by Chinese groups are not credited here but belong to the family, not the original finding.
assessment.maturity: Many independent confirmations and a large literature support the discovery. The pairing mechanism is still unresolved, which weighs against, though the discovery itself is mature and well defined.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism is not understood, which limits the explanatory impact.
Practical impact is modest compared with fundamental importance.
Later contributions (higher Tc groups) are not captured.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength idea and developed by Ye into systems with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, redefine precision measurement and enable tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. The idea is original and the impact lasting.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice concept; Ye led the strontium clock performance advances. Credit seems well supported for these two, though ion-clock and frequency-comb developers have already been honoured (2005) or compete in the same area.
assessment.maturity: Multiple laboratories reproduce and compare clocks at the 1e-18 level, so confirmation is excellent. Timing is plausible given the redefinition of the second under discussion.
uncertainties: Competition for credit with ion clocks (e.g. Al+ clocks) and other lattice groups.
Relationship to the 2005 frequency comb prize.
Dates from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Aberration-corrected electron microscopy brought sub-angstrom imaging of atoms, interfaces and defects in solids and transformed the experimental data available to materials theorists like me. It is an instrumentation advance of broad lasting impact, comparable to the 1986 microscopy prize.
assessment.attribution: Rose provided the optical design, Haider led the corrector construction with Urban's group demonstrating its use, and the three have been jointly honoured elsewhere. The attribution is well anchored; Crewe and others contributed to the history but the trio is coherent.
assessment.maturity: The technique is widely replicated and is a standard tool in laboratories worldwide, so it is mature; prior prize recognition of microscopy raises some question whether it is fitting as physics versus technology.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views the work as physics discovery or engineering.
Contributions from other correction groups (Krivanek, Zach) are not credited here.
Facts about priority from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics established the architecture for strong coupling between superconducting qubits and microwave photons, now central to superconducting quantum computing and quantum-limited readout. It is conceptually clear and its impact is large.
assessment.attribution: Blais proposed the theory, Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in 2004. The names give a clean theory-experiment division, although Devoret and Yale colleagues were also decisive.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups and by large devices, though the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes a closely related award less obviously timely and may be seen as premature to repeat the area.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 prize in superconducting circuits.
Role of other Yale contributors (Devoret, Girvin) in the credit.
Facts from memory.
